headline: Massachusetts collects $5.46 billion in September taxes, beating state benchmark
dek: Preliminary collections were 18.6% above September 2025 and $147 million over the state’s monthly benchmark, putting new focus on the fiscal outlook and November’s revenue-limit vote.
body: Massachusetts collected a preliminary $5.457 billion in tax revenue during September, a strong start to the second quarter of the state’s fiscal year and a figure that exceeded the monthly benchmark by $147 million. The Department of Revenue said the total was $858 million, or 18.6%, higher than September 2025. The figures are preliminary, but they give lawmakers and budget officials an early measure of how the new fiscal year is tracking. The [Massachusetts Department of Revenue](https://www.mass.gov/news/september-revenue-collections-total-5457-billion) released the report Monday.

The gain was spread across several major revenue streams. Income-tax collections totaled $3.234 billion, including $1.586 billion in estimated payments from taxpayers and businesses. Withholding brought in $1.525 billion, sales and use taxes produced $841 million, and corporate and business taxes generated $1.141 billion. Each of those categories was above its September benchmark, although the size of the increases varied. Corporate and business taxes were especially strong compared with last year, rising $447 million, or 64.4%, according to the department’s breakdown.

September is important in the state’s calendar because many individuals and corporations make quarterly estimated payments during the month. The department says roughly 10.2% of Massachusetts’ annual revenue has historically arrived in September, making it the third- or fourth-largest collection month. That seasonal pattern means one strong month cannot by itself establish a full-year trend, especially because later collections can be affected by employment, consumer spending, capital gains, corporate profits and refunds.

Through the first three months of fiscal 2027, Massachusetts had collected approximately $11.700 billion. That is $1.617 billion, or 16%, above the same period in fiscal 2026 and $147 million, or 1.3%, above the year-to-date benchmark. The year-to-date margin is smaller than the headline year-over-year increase because the state’s benchmark is a forward-looking budget estimate rather than a comparison with last year’s actual collections.

The result arrives as state officials and outside analysts debate how much revenue can safely support new spending. The [Massachusetts Taxpayers Foundation’s fiscal forecast](https://masstaxpayers.org/fy-2026-fy-2027-tax-revenue-forecast?field_tags_target_id=130&term_node_tid_depth=All) projects fiscal 2027 non-surtax revenue of about $42.03 billion, an increase of $884 million, or 2.2%, while warning that slower economic growth, flat employment and possible federal funding losses could narrow the state’s cushion. That forecast is not a revision of Monday’s preliminary report; it is a separate outlook that shows why policymakers may treat one strong month cautiously.

The collections also land in the middle of a public debate over Chapter 62F, the state’s tax-revenue limit. Massachusetts voters will decide Question 5 on Nov. 3. As [Boston.com reported](https://www.boston.com/news/politics/2026/09/30/ma-ballot-question-5-explained/?p1=article_recirc_inline_feed), the proposal would reset the starting point for the annual cap to the prior year’s actual collections, apply wage-and-salary growth, and count the state’s 4% surtax on income above $1 million in the calculation. It would apply to fiscal years beginning after June 30, 2027.

A yes vote would not immediately change the amount Massachusetts collects in fiscal 2027, and it would not repeal the millionaires tax. It could, however, make refunds more frequent if collections exceed the revised limit. Boston.com cited Tufts University’s Center for State Policy Analysis, which estimated that the change could produce two to four times as many refunds as the current system, while also warning that the exact amount would depend on future collections and wage growth. Opponents say more frequent refunds could make it harder to plan for education, health care, transportation, housing and public safety.

For households, the September report is not a tax bill or a promise of a refund. It is a snapshot of money already collected by the Commonwealth and a signal about the resources available for the budget process. The most notable uncertainty is whether the strength came from durable gains in wages, sales and business activity or from timing and unusually large estimated payments. The Department of Revenue’s later monthly reports will show whether the margin persists as the fiscal year develops.

The next major checkpoints are the October and November collection reports, followed by the state’s continuing budget updates and the Nov. 3 vote on Question 5. Until those arrive, the clearest conclusion is limited but meaningful: Massachusetts entered fiscal 2027 ahead of its revenue plan, while the state’s own forecasters continue to see enough economic and federal-policy risk to argue against treating September’s surge as money that can automatically be committed.
